specs: Can reach about 8 feet and 300 lb (FWC).

Primarily coastal and inshore as adults, with offshore migrations to spawn. Juveniles commonly occupy estuaries and can use freshwater habitats. The current sources do not establish one universal preferred depth range.

Large, slow-growing coastal migratory fish. Adults concentrate in South Florida during cooler months and are widespread along Florida's coast in summer. Juveniles use estuarine and freshwater nursery habitats; adults migrate offshore to spawn. Tarpon gulp air at the surface and tolerate a wide salinity range.

FWC reports a Florida spawning season of May through September. Florida Museum describes typical spawning in May, June and July and extensive migrations to offshore spawning areas. The Keys spring adult run is a seasonal movement pattern and should not be conflated with the full statewide spawning window.

specs: Can reach about 3 feet and 15-18 lb, though fish over 10 lb are uncommon. FWC reports typical Florida catches averaging roughly 3-5 lb.
Feeds primarily on benthic invertebrates including shrimp, crabs and other small crustaceans found in seagrass and sand-flat sediments.

Shallow-water flats specialist, often in less than one foot of water over seagrass and sometimes white sand. Small schools move across grass and sand flats searching for shrimp, crabs and other invertebrates. Fish are wary and rely on speed and a deeply forked tail. Northern Florida Keys telemetry also documents use of deeper channels that may provide refuge; this does not locate fish in real time.

Some Bahamas studies document spawning-site linkages and seasonal movements, but those findings should not be assumed for South Florida. FWC reports spawning from November through May, probably in deep or offshore water; the timing and routes of individual South Florida spawning migrations remain incompletely understood.

Juveniles use sheltered mangrove-lined swamps, bayous, rivers and creeks; adults use broad estuarine habitat and move between upper-estuary overwintering areas and higher-salinity spawning sites.
Florida spawning generally runs April/May through September/October. Major inlets and coastal river mouths are documented spawning locations. Exact annual timing varies with climate and temperature.

Feeds on fishes, crustaceans and snails.

Coastal waters near structure. Adults commonly use reefs, ledges and shelf-edge habitat; juveniles use shallower vegetated nursery habitats. The existing 25-95 m depth range is not a universal species depth preference and is retained only as a provisional model screening range.

Adults associate with reefs, ledges, wrecks and other structure; juveniles use shallow seagrass and mangrove habitat. In the Florida Keys, adults make seasonal movements to known spawning aggregation sites, including Riley's Hump in the Dry Tortugas. Aggregation locations are discrete and should not be inferred from generic reef polygons.

FWC's Florida species profile reports spawning in July and August. Florida Keys research documents seasonal spawning migrations and aggregations at discrete sites. Full-moon timing and aggregation behavior are location-specific and should not be treated as a universal calendar for all reefs.

specs: Can reach at least 48 inches and 79 lb; sexual maturity is reported around 19 inches for males and 21.5 inches for females. These are maximum/biological reference values, not typical catch sizes.
Benthic feeder that roots through sand and seagrass flats for crabs, shrimp, mollusks and other crustaceans; also takes polychaetes, small fishes and other invertebrates.

Uses shallow sandy and seagrass flats and intertidal areas to forage, often moving onto flats with incoming tides from adjacent channels and basins. Smaller fish commonly school; larger adults are more solitary or occur in pairs. Adults also use wrecks and deeper reef structures. Lower Florida Keys telemetry documents use of both shallow flats and deeper Florida Reef Tract habitat, including reef depths around 15–40 m in the study area.

Lower Florida Keys telemetry reported reef occupancy peaking from March through September, especially April-May, and interpreted this pattern as associated with spawning. Treat this as study-area evidence, not a statewide calendar or proof that every reef polygon is spawning habitat.

specs: Commonly 2-5 lb; FWC reports a maximum around 30 inches and 5 lb. Florida state record: 8 lb 9 oz.
Adults are commonly associated with offshore reef habitat; NOAA Fisheries and stock-assessment sources describe adult use of roughly 10-70 m, while juveniles use shallower nursery habitats.

A reef-associated schooling snapper, commonly found over or near coral reefs and other hard structure. Adults feed on fishes and invertebrates and often rise into the water column to feed. Juveniles use seagrass, mangroves and back-reef nursery habitat.
FWC describes spawning in mid-summer; regional fisheries sources report a broader April-August spawning period in the southeastern United States.
NOAA Fisheries reports a typical lifespan of 6-14 years, with older individuals documented.
